'''Anne Dejean-Assémat''' (born 6 January, 1957) is a French [[Molecular biology|molecular biologist]] working on the mechanisms leading to the development of human [[cancer]]s. Professor at the Pasteur Institute and Research Director at [[Inserm]], she heads the laboratory of Nuclear Organization and Oncogenesis<ref>{{Cite web|last=Institut Pasteur|title=Nuclear Organization and Oncogenesis|url=https://research.pasteur.fr/en/team/nuclear-organization-and-oncogenesis/|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161011120339/https://research.pasteur.fr/en/team/nuclear-organization-and-oncogenesis/|archive-date=2016-10-11|access-date=2016-01-31|website=research.pasteur.fr/}}</ref> at the [[Pasteur Institute]].

== Biography ==
Anne Dejean-Assémat was educated at the [[Pierre and Marie Curie University]] in Paris, graduating with a Master of Science degree in Genetics in 1980. Anne Dejean earned her PhD in 1983 and her habilitation (thèse d'état) in 1988, both from [[Sorbonne University]] (ex [[Pierre and Marie Curie University]]). She got a position at Inserm as Chargée de recherche in 1985 and was appointed head of a Pasteur Institute/Inserm laboratory in 2003. Member of  [[European Molecular Biology Organization|EMBO]], of the [[French Academy of Sciences]] and of the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]], she has received the Gagna and Van Heck Prize, 2003, the [[L'Oréal-UNESCO Awards for Women in Science|Prize L'Oréal-Unesco for Women in Science]], 2010, the [[Inserm|Grand Prix Inserm]], 2014 and the [[Sjöberg Prize]], 2018.

== Scientific contributions ==
A cancer molecular biologist, Anne Dejean-Assémat has contributed several pioneering concepts in the areas of [[Nuclear receptor|nuclear receptors]] and human [[Cancer|cancers]]. She discovered that genes encoding the [[Retinoic acid receptor|receptors for retinoic acid]]  (RAR), the active derivative of [[vitamin A]], are mutated in [[liver cancer]] and in a rare type of [[leukemia]] and deciphered the molecular and cellular bases for the cure of this leukemia, opening up unique perspectives for new [[Cellular differentiation|differentiation]] and [[Targeted therapy|targeted cancer therapy]] leads.{{fact|date=February 2023}} 

She first found such a mutation in a [[Hepatitis B|hepatitis B virus]]-associated liver tumor, demonstrating that this virus, by inserting its genome into that of the hepatic cell, can disrupt neighbouring human genes and directly trigger the development of [[liver cancer]].<ref>{{Cite journal |vauthors=Dejean A, Bougueleret L, Grzeschik KH, Tiollais P |title=Hepatitis B virus DNA integration in a sequence homologous to v-erb-A and steroid receptor genes in a hepatocellular carcinoma|journal=Nature|date=1986 |volume=322 |issue=6074 |pages=70–72|doi=10.1038/322070a0|pmid=3014347 |bibcode=1986Natur.322...70D |s2cid=4355348 }}</ref> This discovery led Dejean-Assémat's team to clone the RARb gene and identify the first responsive element to retinoic acid.<ref>{{Cite journal |vauthors=Brand N, Petkovich M, Krust A, Chambon P, de Thé H, Marchio A, Tiollais P, Dejean A |title=Identification of a second human retinoic acid receptor|journal=Nature|date=1988 |volume=332 |issue=6167 |pages=850–853|doi=10.1038/322070a0|pmid=3014347 |bibcode=1986Natur.322...70D |s2cid=4355348 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |vauthors=De Thé H, Del-Mar-Vivanco-Ruiz M, Tiollais P, Stunnenberg H, Dejean A |title=Identification of a retinoic acid responsive element in the retinoic acid receptor alpha gene|journal=Nature |date=1990 |volume=343 |issue=6254 |pages=177–180|doi=10.1038/343177a0|pmid=2153268 |s2cid=4314508 }}</ref> Together with Hugues de Thé, she then discovered the PML-RARa [[Oncogene|oncoprotein]] as the genetic defect responsible for [[acute promyelocytic leukemia]] (APL) and elucidated its [[Carcinogenesis|oncogenic properties]].<ref>{{Cite journal |vauthors=De Thé H, Chomienne C, Lanotte M, Degos L, Dejean A |title=The translocation of acute promyelocytic leukemia fuses the retinoic acid receptor alpha gene to a novel transcribed locus|journal=Nature |date=1990 |volume=347|issue=6293 |pages=558–561 |doi=10.1038/347558a0|pmid=2170850 |s2cid=4314933 }}</ref><ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |vauthors=de Thé H, Lavau C, Marchio A, Chomienne C, Degos L, Dejean A |title=The PML-RAR alpha fusion mRNA generated by the t(15;17) translocation in acute promyelocytic leukemia encodes a functionally altered RAR|journal=Cell |date=1991 |volume=66 |issue=4 |pages=675–684|doi=10.1016/0092-8674(91)90113-d|pmid=1652369 |s2cid=40272758 }}</ref>

Dejean-Assémat's further work led to the characterization of the mechanisms underlying the cure of APL by [[retinoic acid]]  and [[Arsenic trioxide|arsenic]], a treatment developed in China and that remains the most efficient [[Targeted therapy|oncogene-targeted therapy]]  described so far.<ref>{{Cite journal |vauthors=Hu J, Liu YF, Wu CF, Xu F, Shen ZX, Zhu YM, Li JM, Tang W, Zhao WL, Wu W, Sun HP, Chen QS, Chen B, Zhou GB, Zelent A, Waxman S, Wang ZY, Chen SJ, Chen Z |title=Long-term efficacy and safety of all-trans retinoic acid/arsenic trioxide-based therapy in newly diagnosed acute promyelocytic leukemia|journal=Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A |date=2009 |volume=106 |issue=9 |pages=3342–7|pmc=2651325| doi=10.1073/pnas.0813280106|pmid=19225113 |bibcode=2009PNAS..106.3342H |doi-access=free }}</ref> She showed that therapeutic doses of retinoic acid can correct the deficient molecular response in the leukemic cells.<ref name=":0" /> She also demonstrated that a particular [[organelle]], the PML Nuclear Body, is disrupted in these cells, and that both [[retinoic acid]]  and [[Arsenic trioxide|arsenic]] are able to correct this cellular defect.<ref>{{Cite journal |vauthors=Weis K, Rambaud S, Lavau C, Jansen J, Carvalho T, Carmo-Fonseca M, Lamond A, Dejean A |title=Retinoic acid regulates aberrant nuclear localization of PML-RAR alpha in acute promyelocytic leukemia cells|journal=Cell |date=1994 |volume=76 |issue=2 |pages=345–356|doi=10.1016/0092-8674(94)90341-7 |pmid=8293468 |s2cid=36801773 }}</ref> She then showed that arsenic induces the post-translational modification of PML-RARa by the small SUMO protein as well as the degradation of the oncoprotein.<ref>{{Cite journal |vauthors=Müller S, Matunis MJ, Dejean A |title=Conjugation with the ubiquitin-related modifier SUMO-1 regulates the partitioning of PML within the nucleus|journal=The EMBO Journal |date=1998 |volume=17 |issue=1 |pages=61–70|pmc=1170358|doi=10.1093/emboj/17.1.61|pmid=9427741 }}</ref>

Dejean-Assémat's laboratory next contributed to the emergence of the SUMO field by unveiling an as yet unanticipated function for this pathway as a major [[Epigenetics|epigenetic]] determinant of [[Regulation of gene expression|gene expression regulation]], with a key role in the repression of  [[Innate immune system|innate immunity]]<ref>{{Cite journal |vauthors=Decque A, Joffre O, Magalhaes JG, Cossec JC, Blecher-Gonen R, Seeler JS, Lapaquette P, Silvin A, Joubert PE, Albert ML, Amit I, Amigorena S, Dejean A |title=Sumoylation coordinates the repression of inflammatory and anti-viral gene programs during innate sensing|journal=Nat Immunol |date=2016 |volume=17 |issue=2 |pages=140–149|doi=10.1038/ni.3342|pmid=26657003 |s2cid=12081749 |doi-access=free }}</ref> and the maintenance of cell identity.<ref>{{Cite journal |vauthors=Cossec JC, Theurillat I, Chica C, Búa Aguín S, Gaume X, Andrieux A, Iturbide A, Jouvion G, Li H, Bossis G, Seeler JS, Torres-Padilla ME, Dejean A |title=SUMO Safeguards Somatic and Pluripotent Cell Identities by Enforcing Distinct Chromatin States|journal=Cell Stem Cell |date=November 2018 |volume=23 |issue=5 |pages=742–757 |doi=10.1016/j.stem.2018.10.001|pmid=30401455 |s2cid=205251863 |doi-access=free }}</ref> Her work opened up new avenues in [[regenerative medicine]] and [[Treatment of cancer|cancer treatment]] through pharmacological modulation of sumoylation levels.

3 articles published in Anne Dejean-Assémat's laboratory have been retracted pointing to instances of image manipulation.<ref>{{cite web|title=Retraction|url=http://retractiondatabase.org/RetractionSearch.aspx#?auth%3dDejean%252c%2bAnne|publication-date=}}</ref> In 2019, the Pasteur Institute, CNRS and Inserm launched a joint investigation into research misconduct. The conclusion indicates that one staff scientist of the laboratory, who left the Institut Pasteur in April 2021, had engaged in fraudulent practice.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Scientific integrity communication|url=https://webext.pasteur.fr/welcome/scientific_integrity.pdf |website=Institut Pasteur}}</ref>

== Memberships and awards ==
Anne Dejean-Assémat has held several scientific advisory positions and served in the Scientific Council and as a president of the Genetics, Development and Cancer committee at [[ Inserm]] (2008–2012). She received the  Mergier-Bourdeix Prize of the [[French Academy of Sciences]] (1997), the Rosen Prize from the Medical Research Foundation (1998), the Mitjaville Prize of the [[Académie Nationale de Médecine|National Academy of Medicine]] (1999), the Hamdan Award for Medical Research Excellence - Therapy in Leukemia in 2000,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Dr. Anne Dejean - Sheikh Hamdan Bin Rashid Al Maktoum Award for Medical Sciences - HMA |url=http://www.hmaward.org.ae/profile.php?id=283 |access-date=2023-04-05 |website=www.hmaward.org.ae}}</ref> the Gagna and Van Heck Prize (2003), the Léopold Griffuel Prize from Association de recherche en cancérologie (ARC), (2010),  the [[L'Oréal-UNESCO Awards for Women in Science|Prize L'Oréal-Unesco for Women in Science]],<ref>{{Cite web|title=Prix L'Oréal-Unesco|url=https://www.fondationloreal.com/our-programs-women-science/laureates-loreal-unesco-women-science-international-award |website=Fondation L'Oréal}}</ref> (2010), the Duquesne Prize of la Ligue Nationale Contre le Cancer, (2014), the Grand Prix Inserm<ref>''Anne Dejean-Assémat, is awarded the Inserm Grand Prix for 2014". Newsroom | Inserm. 2014-11-26. Retrieved 2021-08-27.''

https://presse.inserm.fr/en/anne-dejean-assemat-is-awarded-the-inserm-grand-prix-for-2014/17041/</ref> (2014) and the Sjöberg Prize of [[Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences|the Royal Swedish Academy of Science]]<ref>''2018's Sjöberg Prize awarded for unique treatment that cures a once fatal cancer". The Royal Swedish Acacdemy of Science. 5 February 2018. Archived from the original on 10 July 2018.''

https://www.kva.se/en/pressroom/pressmeddelanden/sjobergpriset-2018 {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180710071328/https://www.kva.se/en/pressroom/pressmeddelanden/sjobergpriset-2018 |date=2018-07-10 }}</ref> (2018). She was awarded two Advanced Grants from the [[European Research Council]]  (ERC), in 2011 and 2018. She was appointed Officer in the [[National Order of Merit (France)|Ordre national du Mérite]], (2012) and in the ordre national de la [[Legion of Honour|Légion d'honneur]],<ref>''"Décret du 13 juillet 2016 portant promotion et nomination" :'' https://www.legifrance.gouv.fr/jorf/id/JORFTEXT000032891544</ref> (2016). She was awarded the [[Shaw Prize]] in 2026.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2026-05-27 |title=Announcement Press Conference 2026 Press Release |url=https://www.shawprize.org/en/media/news/announcement-press-conference-2026-press-release |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260527094107/https://www.shawprize.org/en/media/news/announcement-press-conference-2026-press-release |archive-date=2026-05-27 |access-date=2026-05-27 |website=The Shaw Prize}}</ref>

Anne Dejean-Assémat is a member of the [[European Molecular Biology Organization|European Molecular Biology Organisation]] (EMBO) (1995), the [[French Academy of Sciences|French Academy of Science]], (2004), the [[Academia Europaea]] (2005), the European Academy of Cancer Sciences, (2011) and [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences|the American Academy of Arts and Sciences]] (2020).
